Le samedi 12 octobre, des centaines de m: On Saturday, October 12, hundreds of demonstrators marched through downtown Montréal in support of the 10-year-old boy who was allegedly scalded by Stéphanie Borel, a neighbour. The incident has revived fears within the community, which is increasingly questioning the safety of its children. The gathering crystallized a striking moment of solidarity and anger.
Malheureusement, l’attaque dont a été vi: Sadly, the attack on this little boy is not an isolated one. Earlier this year, in July, a two-year-old girl also suffered severe burns at a daycare in Montréal. I still remember the photo in the Journal de Québec: blurred, admittedly, but shocking. In the same way, when I saw the images of the little boy circulating after the incident, they were just as unbearable to look at.
Je n’ai pas pu moi-même couvrir cette ma: I wasn’t able to cover this demonstration myself, so my colleague Aude went. She captured several videos and images that helped me understand the feeling that filled the march: a quest for justice and recognition, and a sense of unfairness over how Black people are treated in our society, but also a search for solidarity among all of Montréal’s Black communities.

<strong>Le samedi 12 octobre, des centai: On Saturday, October 12, hundreds of demonstrators marched through downtown Montréal in support of the 10-year-old boy who was allegedly scalded on October 2 by one of his neighbours, Stéphanie Borel. The incident has revived fears within the community, which is increasingly questioning the safety of its children. La Converse went to the scene to understand their concerns.
C’est une histoire qui semble se répéter: It is a story that seems to keep repeating itself. On October 2, a 10-year-old Black child suffered severe burns to his upper body. Stéphanie Borel, a neighbour living in a building near the intersection of Boulevard Curé-Poirier Est and chemin de Chambly in Longueuil, allegedly threw boiling water on the child simply because he had walked across her property. The boy told Radio-Canada that he was coming home from school with friends and that they had taken a shortcut past Stéphanie Borel’s residence. The child suffered second-degree burns to his body and face. The same day, Stéphanie Borel, 46, was arrested, then released.
Ce drame a été la goutte de trop pour la: This tragedy was the last straw for the Black community, because a few months earlier, in July, <l1>a two-year-old girl also suffered severe burns </l1>after a day at a daycare in Montréal, an incident that had already shaken the community.
En réaction à ces cas d’attaque et maltr: In response to these cases of assault and abuse, a peaceful march was organized on October 12 by the Fédération Africaine et Associations du Canada (FAAC) in collaboration with La Ligue des Noirs de Québec (LNQ). The event brought together the community and its allies, not only to support the little boy but also to demand justice.
<strong>« On veut l’égalité et on la veu: “We want equality, and we wanted it yesterday!”
Le rendez-vous est fixé à la Place Émili: The meeting point was Place Émilie-Gamelin at 2 p.m. About a hundred demonstrators gathered, holding signs and flags in the colours of several African countries. As the march got under way, slogans rang out through the streets of Montréal: “A fairer and safer Quebec for our children,” “Justice for our children,” “Down with racism! Down with injustice!”
Après l’incident, Stéphanie Borel aurait: After the incident, Stéphanie Borel reportedly told the little boy’s father that she acted this way because the young child had been in the habit of knocking on her door for three years. The father disputed this version, since the family only moved into the neighbourhood in January and the boy only started attending the school near the woman’s home a month ago.
Bien que Stéphanie Borel ait été initial: Although Stéphanie Borel was initially arrested by police, she was released the same day on a promise to appear in court next January. The decision sparked outrage within the community.
« Si cela avait été une femme noire qui: “If a Black woman had scalded a white child, things would have gone very differently, and we all know it!” several demonstrators said indignantly.
Sur la place du Canada, le point d'arriv: At Place du Canada, where the march ended, Stanley Bazin, president of the Ligue des Noirs du Québec, took the floor: “We want justice. We don’t want to have to go out and get it, or beg for it,” he began. “We want equality, and we wanted it yesterday!”
Au milieu de la foule, nous rencontrons: In the middle of the crowd, we met Evelyne François, a demonstrator who described herself simply as “a citizen, but also a mother.” She was holding a sign that read: “No to the stigmatization of our Black children.” She was outraged: “We are human beings! We want our rights to be respected! So we have to stand up so that justice is done.” She continued: “This woman deliberately prepared hot water to burn this child. A 10-year-old child, who had done nothing to deserve this! And yet this ‘criminal’ was released while awaiting trial? How is that possible? Where are we headed? What kind of world are we living in?”
Dans ce contexte, la <em>Coalition rouge: In this context, the Coalition rouge, an advocacy group that fights racism, wrote a letter last Thursday to Longueuil Mayor Catherine Fournier and Police Chief Marc Leduc, asking that Stéphanie Borel be placed back in detention. The same day, the mayor of Longueuil said in a statement posted on social media that it was very rare for all the legal criteria to be met to justify detaining a suspect before an investigation has even begun. “Since yesterday, many people have approached me personally about this, urging me to act to reverse the situation (...) as an elected official, I could never ask for a police or judicial decision to be reviewed, much less demand that a person be detained,” she wrote. “That would be illegal.”
Rolande Balma, conseillère municipale du: Rolande Balma, city councillor for the Antoinette-Robidoux district, where the little boy lives, also spoke at a Longueuil city council meeting: “No child and no parent should have to go through such a horrific situation. Of course, the investigation is ongoing, and we will let the justice system decide. But I won’t hide from you that I shed tears when I saw this child’s skin.”
Le lendemain, le vendredi 11 octobre, St: The next day, Friday, October 11, Stéphanie Borel was arrested again “following new evidence obtained in the investigation” against her, the Service de Police de l’Agglomération de Longueuil said in a news release. She has since been “<l1>formally charged with aggravated assault and will remain in custody</l1>,” Radio-Canada reports. It is a more serious charge than the counts of assault causing bodily harm and assault with a weapon that were initially laid. She is expected to remain in custody until at least October 28.
De retour à la place du Canada, plusieur: Back at Place du Canada, several demonstrators denounced a hate crime against the child. But under the law, what really defines such an act, and how can it be proven? We put that question to Fo Niemi, co-founder and executive director of the Center for Research-Action on Race Relations (CRARR), which is dedicated to defending civil rights.
« Selon le Code criminel canadien, un cr: “Under the Criminal Code of Canada, a hate crime is an offence motivated by hatred based on race, religion, sex or other protected characteristics. If such a motivation is proven, it becomes an aggravating factor that increases the sentence,” Fo Niemi began. “However, without solid proof of that motivation, the act will not be classified as a hate crime, which limits the severity of the penalty.”
Cette preuve de motivation est souvent d: Proving that motivation is often difficult, Fo Niemi noted. “That’s what we’ve seen in several cases over the past ten years: the Crown doesn’t always raise this aspect,” he explained. Even when some elements point to a hateful motivation, proving that intent remains a major obstacle in criminal trials. “You really have to examine what the motivation of the person who committed the act was,” Niemi insisted, stressing that this burden falls on the Crown.
En 2023, <l1>Statistiques Canada</l1> a: In 2023, <l1>Statistics Canada</l1> recorded a total of 784 police-reported hate crimes targeting the Black community across the country. Despite a 7% decrease from the previous year, it should be noted that hate crimes against Black people in Canada jumped 96% between 2019 and 2020.
La communauté noire reste la plus touché: The Black community remains the group most affected by hate crimes in the race and ethnic origin category.
Anastasia Marcelin, membre de la ligue d: Anastasia Marcelin, a member of the Ligue des Noirs du Québec, in turn took the floor at Place du Canada: “It’s time to put an end to our divisions. If you don’t wake up now, your children will keep having to fight for their rights!” she declared forcefully. Her voice echoed across the square. She continued: “In 2020, we were here for Black Lives Matter. Today, we’re back because our children are being burned! If we stay inactive, the situation will only get worse. We risk an escalation of violence.” She pointed to a demonstrator in the crowd: “If you don’t move, it’s his children who will have to keep fighting.” The crowd, united, answered in unison: “Solidarity, solidarity!”
Dans cet élan d’unité qui a réuni plusie: In this show of unity that brought together several Black communities, a second march is planned for Saturday, October 26, at 2 p.m., starting from Place Émilie-Gamelin, a FAAC spokesperson announced.
